A hash is a mathematical representation of input into the hash's algorithm. A salt value is a varied value (frequently random string) added to the input. A hash provides the same output for the same input. The use of a salt value means that two users having the same plain text password as input will still generate two distinct hash output values. In this way you can't simply harvest the hash for a single password (which creates a vulnerability into dictionary attacks; looking values for passwords) and use it for a password. You must still have the salt value, per user. Because of this, the salt value is normally also stored with the salted hash inside the database. This combination is used as a password - internally - not from the user.

Regardless, the number one rule is that outside of a development environment, passwords or hashes should never be stored. Period. Anyone violating this rule is a candidate for firing.

As far as I understand the situation, the passwords were logged in plaintext because the logging happened before they were hashed, probably right when the data was initially POSTed from the client side. Logging incoming requests is common for debugging purposes, and apparently someone simply didn't think about passwords being part of the payload being transmitted. Large web entities write gigabytes of logs every day, and nobody really knows what's in them because hundreds of devs log hundreds of minuscule, differing things. That's why entire companies exist that specialise purely on providing tools for log analysis, to make sense of this enormous amount of data at all.

I am willing to attribute this to stupidity instead of malice, as is the case with most things, because this is a mistake everyone can make and it does not make any sense to blame the SJW culture for that. If there was malicious intent behind it, there are many other ways of going about acquiring these passwords, especially without going public about it (or even creating a situation where you'd be forced to do so at all). And to be honest, Twitter does whatever it wants with its users anyway, without the need for any kind of password. That's the thing about being the company who owns the database: You can access it without going through a user's account first. In fact I have to hand out at least a modicum of respect to Twitter for owning up to this transparently (as far as we can tell, anyway) and publicly.
